prompt.context: Our client is BankCoCard, a US credit card subsidiary of the major international bank BankCo. They have a rapidly growing $16 billion credit card portfolio. BankCoCard is interested in lowering their cost of funds for their credit card program by starting an online bank.
prompt.question: BankCoCard would like to know if they should start an online bank and if so, should they launch a savings or a checking account for their new online bank.

clarifying_info.a: BankCoCard wants to launch both a savings and checking account, but their budget only allows for the IT team to build one product this year. Whichever product is not selected will be launched the following year.

clarifying_info.q: How much will it cost to build each product?
clarifying_info.a: The savings and checking accounts are expected to take the same time to build and will cost the same amount to build: $10 million.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current cost of funds?
clarifying_info.a: The current cost of funds is 4% for the credit card portfolio.

clarifying_info.q: Are interest rates expected to change?
clarifying_info.a: Interest rates are not expected to change for the next several years.
Assume all deposits can be lent; no reserves are required.

clarifying_info.q: Where will the online bank operate?
clarifying_info.a: The online bank will only operate within the US.

exhibits.title: Account Info
exhibits.shows: A table comparing key account-level parameters for Checking Account vs. Savings Account across seven dimensions

exhibits.title: Market Info — New Online Accounts Per Year
exhibits.shows: A line chart showing projected new online accounts per year (in millions) from 2016 to 2021, with separate lines for Online Checking Accounts and Online Savings Accounts

data.description: Online Checking Accounts start at ~15 million in 2016 and grow to ~40 million by 2021 (fast growth). Online Savings Accounts start at ~20 million in 2016 and grow more slowly, reaching ~25 million by 2021.

framework: Define the decision: Should BankCoCard launch an online bank, and if yes, which product (savings vs. checking) to launch first?
Assess strategic fit: Does an online bank reduce cost of funds below the current 4%? What are the regulatory and operational requirements?
Evaluate product economics: Compare per-account lifetime profitability for savings vs. checking using revenue and cost drivers
Assess market opportunity: Estimate addressable market size and BankCoCard's realistic capture rate for each product
Consider launch requirements: Upfront build cost, IT timeline, ongoing ops costs, account acquisition strategy
Weigh risks: Market capture uncertainty, reputation risk, regulatory risk, competitive response
Synthesize recommendation: Which product to launch first, and why

questions.prompt: Brainstorm: What upfront costs will there be to launch an online banking product?
questions.guidance: Candidate should generate a broad list across infrastructure, product design, people, and marketing. Strong answers include: website and servers, call center setup, product design and legal/compliance review, employee training, marketing and advertising campaigns.

questions.prompt: Brainstorm: What are the ongoing revenues and costs of a savings account? What additional revenues and costs does a checking account have that a savings account does not?
questions.guidance: Savings revenues: interest income from lending deposits to the credit card portfolio. Savings costs: interest paid to customers, call center, fraud, marketing, statement mailing. Checking additional revenues: overdraft fees, account fees, interchange income, ATM fees. Checking additional costs: debit card transaction processing, ACH transaction processing, ATM reimbursement.

questions.prompt: Brainstorm: What are possible ways of acquiring new accounts for the online banking products? (Aim for at least 4.)
questions.guidance: Strong candidates generate diverse channels: online advertisements, search engine optimization (SEO), affiliate/referral marketing, partnerships (e.g., retailers), cross-selling to existing BankCoCard credit card customers, billboards, event sponsorship, tabling at events.

questions.prompt: Math Q1: The online bank will lend the deposits to the credit card portfolio at a 3% annual interest rate. What is the lifetime profit of a single checking account versus a savings account? (Use Exhibit 1.)
questions.guidance: Candidate must compute lifetime revenue and lifetime costs for each account type, then subtract to get lifetime profit. A strong candidate will ask for a discount rate to NPV future cash flows (acceptable answer: not necessary for this exercise). Checking profit should be ~$280; Savings profit should be ~$110.

math.setup: For each account: Lifetime Profit = Lifetime Revenue - Lifetime Costs. Revenue sources: interest earned on deposits lent to credit card portfolio, plus any fee income. Cost sources: interest paid to depositor, monthly operating expense over account life, account acquisition cost.
math.answer: Checking lifetime profit per account = $280; Savings lifetime profit per account = $110. Checking generates ~2.5x more profit per account.

questions.prompt: Math Q2: Calculate the total lifetime profit of all accounts opened in the first year for both savings and checking products. BankCo expects to capture 10% of the market for whichever product they launch. (Use Exhibit 2.) After computing, what assumptions are you suspicious of?
questions.guidance: Candidate reads the 2016 market size from Exhibit 2 (Savings ~20M, Checking ~15M), applies 10% capture rate, then multiplies by per-account profit. Checking total profit should be ~$420M; Savings should be ~$220M. Strong candidates flag assumptions worth questioning: 10% market capture in year 1 is aggressive, average deposit sizes, account life assumptions, acquisition cost per account.

math.setup: Total Lifetime Profit = Market Size (year 1) * Capture Rate * Per-Account Lifetime Profit
math.answer: Checking total lifetime profit for year-1 cohort = $420 million; Savings = $220 million. Checking generates ~91% more total profit for the first-year cohort.

brainstorming.prompt: What are possible ways of acquiring new accounts for the online banking products?

categories.name: Cross-sell existing base
ideas: Cross-sell to current BankCoCard credit card customers
Email and in-app campaigns to existing cardholders

recommendation: BankCoCard should start an online bank and launch the checking account in the first year, followed by the savings account in the second year
The checking account generates nearly twice the lifetime profit of the savings account ($280 vs. $110 per account) and nearly twice the total first-year cohort profit ($420M vs. $220M)
The online checking market is also growing faster than the savings market (CAGR ~20% vs. ~10%), providing a larger long-run opportunity

Note for an especially strong candidate: the original objective is to lower cost of funds (currently 4%). Savings accounts would generate ~$10B in deposits ($5,000 avg * 2M accounts) vs. ~$3B for checking ($2,000 avg * 1.5M accounts), providing more volume to fund the credit card portfolio. A sophisticated candidate would weigh this against the profit differential and may recommend savings first on strategic grounds.
risks: BankCoCard may capture less than 10% of the market in year one — this assumption is aggressive for a new entrant
Reputation risk: a failed or poorly-executed online banking launch could damage the BankCo brand
Account acquisition costs could be higher than modeled, compressing per-account economics
The product may not be sufficiently differentiated from established online banks (e.g., Ally, Marcus)
Regulatory and compliance risk associated with launching a new online banking charter or product
next_steps: Meet with regulators to understand licensing, compliance, and capital requirements
Survey potential customers to inform product design and feature priorities
Collect industry reports to validate market size and growth assumptions
Interview industry experts and potential banking partners
Host focus groups to test product concepts
Hire IT staff and begin website design
Request additional budget to enable both products to be built concurrently
Establish a call center and train customer service staff
